In most cases, the effort to return home ends short of its goal. An exciting beginning often gives way to a disappointing conclusion. When successful, the journey home is likely to require several stops, careful patience, and occasional risk. Rare is the journey home that simply requires a short touch of each of the bases. Further, the journey home does not have a timeclock. Each journey proceeds at its own unique pace. To find home, get home, return home is a profoundly human hope, and a deeply spiritual longing. Many of the great hymns of our faith are in touch with this longing. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council and city staff. Editor: I am writing on behalf of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont regarding the 2021 Alameda County Grand Jury Report on “The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions.” A copy of the report is attached and can also be found online at http://grandjury.acgov. org/grandjury-assets/docs/2020- 2021/Ballot%20Measures.pdf. The grand jury’s report focused on the accuracy, transparency and impartiality of government sponsored ballot questions. They found that ballot questions suffer from “proponent’s bias” and fall short of what voters have a right to expect in terms of truthfulness and impartiality. The League supports transparency in local government and there are few better examples for the necessity for transparency than in the language of a government sponsored ballot question. Language that is biased, unclear, or unnecessary falls short of our expectations for a fair and transparent government. Looking specifically at the example of Piedmont’s Measure TT, the grand jury found that the ballot question contained language that was irrelevant or unnecessary to describe the measure. The grand jury also found that because of the irrelevant or unnecessary language that delineated specific spending, Measure TT could have been mistaken by voters to propose a special tax instead of the general tax that it is. This is especially troubling because approval of general tax measures requires only a simple majority whereas special tax measures require a two-thirds majority. Both the League’s published a Pros & Cons document and the City Attorney’s Impartial Analysis of Measure TT stated, “[funds] generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used for any City general revenue purpose.” We know that not all voters have access to nor will be able to read these additional resources prior to casting a ballot. It is important for voters that language of the ballot question itself be unbiased and clear. We hope that the City of Piedmont will ensure that the language of future ballot questions addresses the concerns set forth in the grand jury report. We are copying the Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education on this letter so they may also keep these principles in mind when sponsoring ballot measures in the future. The League stands ready to assist in any efforts that will result in a more fair and transparent local government. Lorriel A. Plimier is President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont.
articles.title: Grand Jury raises questions about ballot measures

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department, in an ongoing effort to increase transparency and meet the community’s needs, has introduced its strategic plan for 2021-2024 to the public. The plan outlines priorities and objectives aligned with the department’s vision, mission, and values in providing police services, pro- “This strategic plan represents the collaborative efforts of many people who took the time and had the trust to engage in open and honest conversations about community safety in our city,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. He explained that it comes at a critical time in Piedmont’s history, as residents navigate a pandemic, environmental challenges, and address social equity issues, especially following the murder of George Floyd by former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin in May 2020. “While the outcomes of these challenges are not known, we are confident that our partnerships, openness, and accountability will position the department to meet the current day challenges as well as challenges yet to come,” he said. The outlined plan includes planning processes, team building, key imperatives, external communication engagement, and policing and legislative reforms. Ongoing strategy efforts, including the evaluation and assessment of the Juvenile Officer program, are also outlined. The department consulted the professional services of Dr. Marilyn Manning to gather input from the community, police department staff and city employees when developing the plan. Focus group sessions represented members of the community to include Piedmont seniors, Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and Piedmont Anti-Racism Diversity Committee (PADC), the school district, worship communities and more. “We want to be transparent with you, our residents, about our police department’s policies and procedures. We acknowledge that, while we strive to employ progressive policies and a culture of accountability among our ranks, we can always do better,” Bowers said. articles.text: PPD invites residents to display their classic cars Sept. 6 The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. The lineup of cars will be in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. The last time the event was held in 2019, 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. From classic cars to late model Ferraris and Bugattis, the vehicles and owners will be there ready to show to car buffs. Coffee will be served, and neighbors are invited to meet members of the police department while viewing and chatting with the car owners. The event is part of the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign, which was started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law enforcement members. In 2018 the Piedmont Police Department decided to rev up the event by adding classic cars to the mix. The community responded enthusiastically, and more than 1600 people showed up. Officer Tyler Petit is coordinating the show. Piedmont residents interested in participating in the city’s version of the unofficial Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. Piedmont residents are invited to enter their classic cars in the 3rd annual PPD Car Show, sponsored by the police department on Labor Day morning, September 6. Above is a 1954 Mercury Sport Coup owned by Robert Walz; one of the 44 cars that participated in the 2019 event.
articles.title: 3rd annual Car Show coming on Labor Day

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Police and Piedmont Fire Departments visited five neighborhoods with BBQ events on Tuesday, August 3 during the city’s annual National Night Out event. More than 100 residents came out for the event which is designed to unite neighbors and to familiarize them the police and fire officials. National Night Out began in 1984, and now has over 10,000 communities participating in the event. The fire department brought out their fire engines and the police sent 13 officers and dispatchers around town to events held at Waldo and Blair, Cavanaugh Court, Ranleigh Way, Huntleigh Road, and the roundabout at Alta and Scenic. Most locations had 15-20 participants. The largest get together was at Waldo and Blair, which had around 60 residents partaking in the festivities. A taco truck was stationed at the Waldo Avenue event organized by resident Marilyn Weber. “There was great attendance at each location,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, “As soon as I got out of the car I had really great dialogues. Rich communication and discussions resulted from residents’ interesting questions.” Bowers credited Police Captain Chris Monahan and Officer Nicole Casalnuovo for their work organizing the events. Bowers was pleasantly surprised with the popularity of the event and found himself watching his wristwatch to make sure he had enough time to visit all the locations between 5:00 and 8:00 p.m. Police Department Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas is in charge of the Department’s social media outreach which Bowers started in 2016. Her participation in the event gave the department valuable takeaways about community communications. “She found that even though it feels like we are putting out a lot of communication on our social media accounts, it was amazing the amount of times people expressed that they weren’t aware of what we are doing.” Bowers said. He acknowledged that outreach to the community through events like this and in print journalism helps reach sectors of the community social media does not. articles.text: On July 22, the Piedmont High Adventure Crew (HAC), a coed teen Venture unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, went on a 5-day backpacking trip in eastern Yosemite National Park. With Lisa Gros, Mike Bandrowski and Bryan Gros as adult leaders, a group of five teens drove to Mono Village Resort in Toiyabe National Forest, where they camped overnight before their hike. The following morning, they headed into Hoover National Wilderness for a steep uphill 2,500-foot climb 8-1/2 miles to Peeler Lake at an elevation of 9,500 feet. To refuel after a long day of hiking, they cooked vegetable curry for dinner and snacked on some marshmallows for dessert. On day 2, they descended 1,600 feet over an 8-mile hike to the sandy shores of Benson Lake in Yosemite National Park, where they camped for two nights. For Valerie Xiong, a 4-year crew member and the camp chef, the trek to the lake was a highlight of the trip. “It was just miles of verdant valley with wildflowers lining the trail and mountains all around. Jasper Zietlow takes in the view from Volunteer Peak. The natural beauty of the High Sierra always amazes me,” she said. On the third day the crew went on a short hike following a stream up to a nearby pass. In the afternoon, it began to rain, so they bonded by holding an informal talent show under the shelter of a stand of lodgepole pines. The morning after, they got up early to retrace their steps, starting with a steep hike out of Benson Lake. After completing an additional seven miles through the meadows of Yosemite, the group arrived again at the clear water of Peeler Lake, where they went for a refreshing swim. It began to rain heavily that night, so the teens huddled together in a tent to watch Free Solo, a rock-climbing movie one of the hikers had downloaded onto a phone. One of the best aspects of the High Adventure Crew backpacking trips is getting to know the other people on the trip. pages.text: Wednesday, August 11, 2021 11 High Adventure Crew goes backpacking in Yosemite By Clare Murphy On July 22, the Piedmont High Adventure Crew (HAC), a coed teen Venture unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, went on a 5-day backpacking trip in eastern Yosemite National Park. With Lisa Gros, Mike Bandrowski and Bryan Gros as adult leaders, a group of five teens drove to Mono Village Resort in Toiyabe National Forest, where they camped overnight before their hike. The following morning, they headed into Hoover National Wilderness for a steep uphill 2,500-foot climb 8-1/2 miles to Peeler Lake at an elevation of 9,500 feet. To refuel after a long day of hiking, they cooked vegetable curry for dinner and snacked on some marshmallows for dessert. On day 2, they descended 1,600 feet over an 8-mile hike to the sandy shores of Benson Lake in Yosemite National Park, where they camped for two nights. For Valerie Xiong, a 4-year crew member and the camp chef, the trek to the lake was a highlight of the trip. “It was just miles of verdant valley with wildflowers lining the trail and mountains all around. Jasper Zietlow takes in the view from Volunteer Peak. The natural beauty of the High Sierra always amazes me,” she said. On the third day the crew went on a short hike following a stream up to a nearby pass. In the afternoon, it began to rain, so they bonded by holding an informal talent show under the shelter of a stand of lodgepole pines. The morning after, they got up early to retrace their steps, starting with a steep hike out of Benson Lake. After completing an additional seven miles through the meadows of Yosemite, the group arrived again at the clear water of Peeler Lake, where they went for a refreshing swim. It began to rain heavily that night, so the teens huddled together in a tent to watch Free Solo, a rock-climbing movie one of the hikers had downloaded onto a phone. Piedmont High senior JoJo Murphy walks into his final year at the school with some nice credits. He recently was named Bay Area Basketball Athlete of the Year by WestCoastPreps.com. “Watching him was just like watching Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson during their many, many, many flurries on the basketball court. Both teams are coached by Howard Oliver, entering his fourth year at the helm. The boys’ team had a particularly strong season earlier this year, finishing with a 16-2 record. Both teams placed 3rd in the 2021 WACC League Tournament at Monarch Bay in San Leandro. The boys had a strong roster of four seniors: Milo Filler, Henry Lambert, Nate Wilson, and Salem Cavenaugh. Oliver had high hopes for them, with the possibility of a league championship. “Lambert, Wilson, Filler, and Cavenaugh – those guys are second-gen golfers but multisport athletes. That’s really why it worked. I came in when they were sophomores. Wilson and Lambert were really serious about the game,” said Oliver. The older players helped recruit Anders Payne and Max “Popcorn” Schleuning. “They were all falling in love with golf, and they have really built the program. With Covid they were chomping at the bit to do something, so they were at the golf course. Anders and Max came out, and they just fit in,” said Oliver. But the team went played in the league championship tournament on May 24 without two of its top players, Lambert and Cavenaugh, due to an AP test and an injury respectively. Regardless, the Highlanders placed third with 456 strokes. Alameda was second with 447, and Castro Valley won with a 389. Wilson led the team with a 77, 6 over par at Monarch Bay. Filler shot an 88, Payne had ant 89, and Schleuning shot a 94. Nico Koh had a 108, and Nate Hart 116. Payne and Schleuning enter their senior years as team leaders. Girls team The girls’ team hopes to challenge Alameda and its 16-year reign as league champions. Aryana Fisher enters her junior year returns as team captain, joining senior Dabney Warner as a returning varsity player. The team includes junior Rahimeen Shah, seniors Toby Jacob and Abigail Drake. A group of freshmen could make an impact as well. “This is going to be the best team the school has had in a while. Every year they make a sweatshirt, and only starters get to wear it, I think that’s something we could start offering to the community,” said Oliver. The team lost three players to graduation earlier this year: Maddie Schaefer, Emily Adams, and Madeleine Meaux. Adams will return as an assistant coach. “Emily is going to come back as an assistant before she goes off to college. To me that says she sees talent down the line, she loves what we built and is proud to be a part of it,” said Oliver. articles.text: The Dixie Fire has escalated to 487,764 acres as of August 10 as it wages through Butte, Lassen, Plumas, and Tehama counties. It is now the largest single-source fire in California history and has obliterated the historic town of Greenville. As of August 10, 893 residential or commercial structures have been destroyed with another 14,000 being threatened. The fire is 25% contained according to Cal Fire. With fire season, the subsequent impact on air quality can quickly blanket areas with smoke. Luckily for the Bay Area, the winds off the Pacific are currently keeping the East Bay in the green. However, inland winds typically pick up in the fall and could keep smoke in the Bay Area similar to September 2020. Hikers in the Lake Tahoe region er faced with an air quality index of 122, deemed unhealthy, with a forecast of only a moderate range for the next week. The air quality in Yosemite Valley was 76 and was forecasted to stay in the moderate range until clearing up this weekend, August 14-15. East Bay Regional Park District East Bay Regional Park District announced on July 14 that it received a grant of $13.5 million from the State for wildfire prevention, with $10 million specifically earmarked for addressing the issue of sudden tree die-off. EBRPD will provide further study on tree die-off in its parks and replace fire equipment including an aging helicopter. “[We will] specifically remove dead and dying trees in Regional Parks, a new tree mortality phenomenon occurring in several parklands,” explained EBRPD Fire Chief Aileen Theile. “$3.5 million of the State appropriation was proposed to provide for fire equipment that will improve the Park District’s ability to fight fires, including the replacement of its aging helicopter which is relied upon as a primary tool to drop water on fires burning in inaccessible terrain.” “EBRPD has more than 1,500 acres of dead or dying trees affected by drought and climate change conditions that need immediate attention,” she said. “These State funds couldn’t come at a better time, as we are shovel ready with designated projects to remove dangerous fuels in District parks while helping to keep forests healthy.”
articles.title: East Bay Regional Park District receives $13.5 million for fire prevention

The sung-and-rapped musical tells the story of American Founding Father Alexander Hamilton. Miranda said he was inspired to write the musical after reading Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography of Hamilton. The show draws heavily from pop, soul, hip-hop, and a traditional style of show tunes. It received Tony Awards for Best Musical and Best Original Score, and a Pulitzer Prize for Best Drama. The musical routinely receives rave reviews in publications across the U.S. and abroad. A review in The Economist in London summed up the response to Hamilton as “near-universal critical acclaim.” The original Broadway cast recording received a 2016 Grammy Award for Best Musical Theatre Album. The show runs for two hours and 45 minutes and includes one intermission. The musical is produced by Jeffrey Seller, Sander Jacobs, and Jill Furman; the fourweek performance is directed by Thomas Kail with choreography by Andy Blankenbuehler and musical supervision by Alex Lacamoire. The show is recommended for ages 10 and up due to strong language. Anyone 15 and under must be accompanied by an adult attending the same performance, and no children under age 5 are allowed. All ticket holders, regardless of age, are required to show proof of full COVID vaccination or negative test results from a COVID PCR test, taken within 72 hours of performance time, for entry into the theatre. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts The Piedmont Center for the Arts is celebrating its 10th Anniversary with Festival Days, a two-month series of music and art events in August and September. Festival Days begins on Sunday, August 15, with a special string quartet concert presented by the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, an ensemble that has performed previously at the Center. The first public exhibition of art of the late local artist Martha Dickson Skinner Gerardo will be on view in an extensive retrospective. The following two weekends will include performances by the Piedmont Troubadours vocal a capella chamber group, blues guitarist Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules, a jazz trio led by Benjamin Ring, and a spectacular viola recital. During Festival Days in September there will be performances by a well-known local violinist and a classical guitarist against the backdrop of an art quilt exhibition exploring the concept of hope through times of wildfires and Covid. articles.text: Pianist Mark Anderson, Piano Chair at the University of British Columbia, performed a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon. The Piedmont Center for the Arts opened to public concerts on Sunday afternoon in grand style. The walls were festively decorated with a spectacular photography exhibit by Virginia Hong. The Piedmont Troubadours opened the festivities with a brief set of a cappella singing. Raconteur extraordinaire Jonathan Dimmock spoke briefly and told the audience how all of the arts are connected. Hong, a San Francisco photographer, is very self-effacing about her art. She has traveled the world and is able to capture these peregrinations vividly. The photos are absolutely natural and not enhanced in any way. When she takes pictures of animals, she lies and waits for them to create the remarkable images she is able to capture. That is part of the beauty of her art. Another part is the beautiful presentation. It was an exhibition worth seeing, and unfortunately ended after Sunday’s concert. The musical part of the afternoon opened with the Piedmont Troubadors. They are, as always, a delight. I heard them not long ago in an impromptu alfresco program at a neighbor’s home. This time they sang indoors with a completely different program. They convey the joy of singing which makes them one of Piedmont‘s treasures.

articles.text: Festival Opera continues its 30th Anniversary Season with the world premiere of “A Jake Heggie Triptych” featuring the award-winning composer and pianist live, this Friday on August 13. Another performance will be held on August 15, both at the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. The world premiere will feature three song cycles, reimagined as fully-staged operas. For these two productions, composer and pianist Jake Heggie is joined by acclaimed singers Carrie Hennessey, Diana Tash, award-winning actor Curt Branom and Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. The song cycles are reimagined as fully-staged chamber operas. The Triptych is the result of Gordin’s long relationship with Heggie’s music. “I’ve been a huge fan of Jake’s work since the release of his ‘The Faces of Love’ [1999] album, which featured many dear colleagues and friends. I was immediately struck by his ability to build a whole environment with his piano writing, how operatic in nature it is, like the music provides both an orchestra and scenery,” Gordin said. “As a singer Opera composer Jake Heggie who is always looking for the essential truth in the music and stories I’m telling, it was a revelation to see his vocal writing truly mirroring the inflection, joy, and pathos of the human voice with honesty, setting texts in an immediately accessible, and deeply compelling way.” “I’m thrilled and deeply honored that Festival Opera will present this dynamic triptych of my compositions, beautifully cast with stunning performers,” Heggie said. “The human quest for identity and connection links this trio of works, which were created with my most frequent collaborators – Gene Scheer and the late, great American playwright Terrence McNally. What a dream for this to unfold in the East Bay, where long ago I studied piano as a teenager.” Triptych will have a live performance on Friday, August 13 at 7:30 p.m. and on Sunday, August 15 at 2:00 p.m. in the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. Tickets are available at: https://www.festivalopera.org/ajake-heggie-triptych.

articles.text: Julia Roberts and Lucas Hedges in a scene from Ben is Back. Drug addiction – in Ben is Back it’s opioids – is the equivalent of dropping a stone into a still pond and bearing witness to the fact that what takes place is not just about that singular stone vanishing beneath the surface, but about the ripples that follow, moving ever outward in concentric circles. The metaphor conveys that the addict does not walk his or her path alone, but often leaves a wake of fragmented ruin. In Ben is Back the addict is 19-year-old Ben Burns who unexpectedly appears at his family’s upstate New York home, having left rehab. He is standing in the front yard as his mother, Holly (Julia Roberts), and his three siblings drive up and see him (he is part of a blended, multiracial family). Holly whispers, “It’s Ben” and immediately gets out of the car and runs toward him. Ben is back. Her son. Her pure pleasure at seeing him is conveyed explicitly as she pulls him warmly into her embrace. It’s only after this moment of surprised joy passes that she steps back, never losing contact with him, and asks, “Ben, what are you doing here?” Ben’s answer is all but lost as he mumbles something about his counselor giving him permission, it’s Christmas, and this is home. Holly yearns to believe him and wants above all for this return to mean that he is who he was, free of the insidious, coextensive, addictive cycle while simultaneously realizing that Ben’s many betrayals, his constant dissembling, cannot be simply put away or erased. Should he be allowed to stay? Should she or her husband, Neal (Courtney B. Vance), who has arrived home, drive him back to rehab? It’s Christmas Eve, and they agree to let him stay for a day. His younger teen sister, Ivy (Kathryn Newton), is far more pessimistic about this decision. She knows (as do Holly and Neal, absent denial), with a heart shriveling truth that they have all stood in this place before while wishing the outcome would be different. The harrowing story of Ben’s return is played out over 24 hours as he is confronted with the cascade of harm his addiction has done, not only to himself, but his family, as well as others in the community, meaning those, innocent and criminal, he has used to ladder himself to the next pill. As Dean says: if Ben were black he would be in jail and not in costly rehab. What carries every frame of Ben is Back is the very fine performance of Julia Roberts. She moves across a spectrum of emotions, from loving Ben fully, to worry, to anger, to rage, mixed with a helpless fear that the grip of addiction will again assert itself and overwhelm Ben’s ability to resist and will again be just beyond her reach. It’s Roberts who must access the full panoply of maternal emotions, made evident by an overwhelming sense of sadness leavened by defeat. In one evocative scene, out of desperation, she drives Ben to a cemetery and asks him where, among the gray tombstones, he wishes to be buried. It’s a remarkable performance; perhaps the best in what has been a long, memorable career. There is one irrefutable fact that should be acknowledged regarding Ben is Back. This family is affluent and able to pay for Ben’s treatment. All of his life he has been nurtured by those who love him. His smile is wide and bright, his skin unblemished. While the maternal love conveyed by Holly is universal, the fate that awaits those who fall into this dark chasm of addiction (for Ben it was a doctor’s prescription) the outcome can be starkly different, often defined by an unrelenting poverty, isolation, devoid of help or options and too often results in a cold, lonely death. Ben is Back. Directed by Peter Hedges. Starring Lucas Hedges, Julia Roberts, Courtney B. Vance. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated R.

articles.text: August and September tickets almost sold out San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now displaying an immersive art exhibition entitled “teamLab: Continuity.” The art experience immerses patrons in a “wondrous ecosystem of lush imagery drawn from nature and East Asian art that dynamically evolves around you.” Rich hues are displayed dramatically via light-work onto the museum’s walls, in sumptuous images of crows, flowers, butterflies, fish, and more imagery. The Tokyo-based artist-collective teamLab is known for producing interactive, interconnected digital artworks that marry art and technology. “Everything exists in a long, fragile, yet miraculous borderless continuity of life,” teamLab founder Toshiyuki Inoko said. The exhibition is designed to be an immersive experience – not about the digital realm, but instead about the natural world. Due to popular demand, the exhibition was extended into September, but tickets are limited and nearly sold out. Fall admission for “teamLab: Continuity” will be released on Thursday, August 19, at 8 a.m. Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/teamlab-continuity/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: A scene fron Disney’s Wreck-It Raph. The premise of Wreck-It Ralph is not only retro, but decidedly creative and fun. The story is set in a suburban arcade filled with games, a place where the neighborhood cool kids hang out during the day. But here’s the best part: when the arcade shuts down for the night, and the kids have all gone home, it’s transformed into an enchanting world where the game characters come to life and socialize. One of the video game meanies is Wreck-It-Ralph (John C. Reilly), a nemesis in a game called Fix-ItFelix Jr. Ralph is a big, hulking guy with oversized hands and feet who smashes buildings, while Felix (Jack Brayer) follows closely behind with his magic hammer, repairing the damage. Ralph has been wrecking the same building for years, day after day. Of course, he always faces the threat of the Newlanders, hostile residents who live in the building Ralph is wrecking. Meanwhile, Ralph sleeps in a garbage dump when he’s not wrecking stuff, using a tree stump for a pillow. For Ralph, it’s a lonely, sad life and he wants out. So Ralph abandons his game to try out others. The problem is that when he doesn’t return the kids think Fix-It-Felix Jr. is broken. Felix is therefore desperate to find Ralph and get him to come back so he’ll have things to fix. Meanwhile, Ralph is wandering from game to game. As it turns out, he spends a lot of time in a game called Sugar Rush where he becomes friends with Vanellope von Schweetz (Sarah Silverman) who has been prevented by despot King Candy and a group of mean girls from competing in the go-cart races. Both Vanellope and Ralph are unhappy and want to break free of their games’ programs. The story has a nice finale, involving a gateway to the inner arcade, called Arcade Central, while introducing a bevy of characters. There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the pleasure of kids. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. Walt Disney Animation. Directed by Rich Moore. With the voices of John C. Reilly, Sarah Silverman, and Jack McBrayer. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: A scene fron Pixar’s Ratatouille. As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who, along with his large family, plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, “Eat your garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his newfound friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy is now the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. Pixar’s use of names brings a smile to the faces of its adult viewers: Linguini as a dishwasher in a restaurant; Ego as the food critic. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. Of course, there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. And, not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time giving the restaurant a glowing review. The story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios. The colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story is one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille (2007). Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G.
articles.title: Ratatouille – another gem from Pixar to savor

articles.text: John Arns and Sandy Belcher, owners and winemakers of Arns Winery. Arns is a tiny 10-acre vineyard on the hillside of the Eastern hills of Howell Mountain near St. Helena. While it was originally a farmstead in the late 1880’s, its modern incarnation began in the late 1950’s when the Arns family bought the property. John Arns and Sandi Belcher, both UC Davis trained enologists, developed Arns Winery after years of selling grapes to local wineries. Their hillside vineyard is planted to seven different clones of Cabernet Sauvignon which are farmed using organic methods. When I first tasted an Arns Cabernet Sauvignon years ago, I knew I had discovered something special. Its intense blackberry fruit, chocolate and leather aromas and flavors were enchanting. To me, the current Cabernets continue in that tradition and they are classic, textbook examples of what Napa Valley Cabernet should be. Arns’ total production is 2000 cases. The best way to buy the wine is directly from the winery website. www.arnswinery.com. (707) 963 3429. • 2018 Arns Chardonnay Searby Vineyard The lovely wine from the Sonoma Coast region exhibits great richness, a fabulous bouquet of flowers, quince, peaches and delicate spicy oakiness that is restrained but present. Broad, full-bodied, multi-dimensional and intense, this is a delicious wine that should drink well for up to 10 years. • 2011 Arns Cabernet Sauvignon Estate Medium garnet-purple colored, the 2011 Cabernet Sauvignon Estate features notes of cranberries, raspberries, and red currants with touches of earth, and wild thyme. Medium bodied and elegant with understated tannins and a lovely freshness, it finishes with pleasant herb and toast flavors. This is the perfect age to drink this wine. • 2012 Arns Cabernet Sauvignon Estate Medium to deep garnet in color, the 2012 Cabernet offers up aromas of blackberry and plums with touches of herbs and forest floor. It is round and full in the mouth. Medium bodied it has a velvety backbone stuffed with red and blue fruits, finishing long and earthy. A perfect partner to a grilled rib-eye steak. • 2013 Arns Cabernet Sauvignon Estate The 2013 offers wonderful black and blue fruit notes that come bounding out of the glass – blueberry pie, cassis, plums – with hints of chocolate, tobacco and earth. In the mouth Arns 2018 Chardonnay The Arns Cabernet vineyard on the side of Howell Mountain.

articles.text: A chopped salad with creamy feta dressing is perfect for warm summer days. If zesty, tangy, and salty flavors please your palate, this salad is an excellent accompaniment to a summer lunch or dinner. Our Piedmont summer days are relatively mild, but plenty of readers live where daytime temps soar above 100°F. A cold, refreshing salad may just make the meal. Farmers markets are brimming with all these vegetables. Tomatoes and cucumbers are at their peak, and every week I see more varieties and larger displays. I encourage bringing feta cheese into your rotation of cheeses if it’s not already. Traditionally made from sheep’s milk (or a combination of sheep and up to 30% goat’s milk), feta is tangy and salty due to being brined. It’s a semi-hard cheese so it crumbles and melts well. Buying a small, plain block provides ultimate flexibility in uses, compared to the myriad options of crumbled and cubed, plain and flavored. If you purchase your block of cheese packaged in its brine, be sure to save the brine to store any unused cheese. It will keep well in the refrigerator, so long as it’s completely submerged in brine. As always, experiment with different tastes and textures. Adding or substituting cubes of watermelon, avocado, and whole prepared garbanzo beans, pickled Greek peperoncini, or boiled new potatoes would be right at home here. Also consider including a protein such as cold chicken, tuna, or sliced hard boiled eggs. INGREDIENTS Dressing Makes about 3/4 cup, enough for one salad, plus leftovers • 3 ounces feta cheese, cut into 1/ 2-inch cubes • 1/2 cup Greek yogurt, plain, whole milk • 1–2 cloves garlic, chopped, to taste • 1 tablespoon lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 1–2 teaspoons white wine vinegar, to taste • 2 tablespoons whole milk, more or less for desired consistency • Freshly ground black pepper, to taste • Scant salt, to taste (feta is already salty) Combine the first six ingredients into the bowl of a minifood processor, blender jar, or small, deep bowl if using a handheld blender. Start with a few pulses, then blitz until smooth. Add small amounts of milk, blending after each addition, until the dressing has a smooth, creamy consistency. Adjust seasoning, remembering you want a fairly strong flavor to “dress” the salad. Note: It will be up to you to determine the consistency of the dressing with the amount of milk you add. I prefer mine about the consistency of ketchup. Salad • 1/4 to 1/2 cup red onions, sliced. (See note.) • 1–2 tomatoes, cut into 1-inch pieces • 1–2 cucumbers, sliced into 3/ 4-inch pieces • 1/2 cup Kalamata olives, pitted • 1/4 cup f lat leaf parsley, chopped • 2 tablespoons fresh mint, chopped Put all salad ingredients into a large bowl and stir gently to combine. Mix in creamy feta dressing to taste. Note: If you prefer to tame the bite from raw, red onion, marinate them in a simple mix of 1 tablespoon each of white wine vinegar and olive oil, plus salt and pepper. Set aside while you prepare the dressing and are ready to assemble the salad. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

A chopped salad with creamy feta dressing is perfect for warm summer days. By Deborah Quok If zesty, tangy, and salty flavors please your palate, this salad is an excellent accompaniment to a summer lunch or dinner. Our Piedmont summer days are relatively mild, but plenty of readers live where daytime temps soar above 100°F. A cold, refreshing salad may just make the meal. Farmers markets are brimming with all these vegetables. Tomatoes and cucumbers are at their peak, and every week I see more varieties and larger displays. I encourage bringing feta cheese into your rotation of cheeses if it’s not already. Traditionally made from sheep’s milk (or a combination of sheep and up to 30% goat’s milk), feta is tangy and salty due to being brined. It’s a semi-hard cheese so it crumbles and melts well. Buying a small, plain block provides ultimate flexibility in uses, compared to the myriad options of crumbled and cubed, plain and flavored. If you purchase your block of cheese packaged in its brine, be sure to save the brine to store any unused cheese. It will keep well in the refrigerator, so long as it’s completely submerged in brine. As always, experiment with different tastes and textures. Adding or substituting cubes of watermelon, avocado, and whole prepared garbanzo beans, pickled Greek peperoncini, or boiled new potatoes would be right at home here. Also consider including a protein such as cold chicken, tuna, or sliced hard boiled eggs. INGREDIENTS Dressing Makes about 3/4 cup, enough for one salad, plus leftovers • 3 ounces feta cheese, cut into 1/ 2-inch cubes • 1/2 cup Greek yogurt, plain, whole milk • 1–2 cloves garlic, chopped, to taste • 1 tablespoon lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 1–2 teaspoons white wine vinegar, to taste • 2 tablespoons whole milk, more or less for desired consistency • Freshly ground black pepper, to taste • Scant salt, to taste (feta is already salty) Combine the first six ingredients into the bowl of a minifood processor, blender jar, or small, deep bowl if using a handheld blender. Start with a few pulses, then blitz until smooth. Add small amounts of milk, blending after each addition, until the dressing has a smooth, creamy consistency. Adjust seasoning, remembering you want a fairly strong flavor to “dress” the salad. Note: It will be up to you to determine the consistency of the dressing with the amount of milk you add. I prefer mine about the consistency of ketchup. Salad • 1/4 to 1/2 cup red onions, sliced. (See note.) • 1–2 tomatoes, cut into 1-inch pieces • 1–2 cucumbers, sliced into 3/ 4-inch pieces • 1/2 cup Kalamata olives, pitted • 1/4 cup f lat leaf parsley, chopped • 2 tablespoons fresh mint, chopped Put all salad ingredients into a large bowl and stir gently to combine. Mix in creamy feta dressing to taste. Note: If you prefer to tame the bite from raw, red onion, marinate them in a simple mix of 1 tablespoon each of white wine vinegar and olive oil, plus salt and pepper. Set aside while you prepare the dressing and are ready to assemble the salad. articles.text: If you’ve had an IRA and a 401(k) for many years, you may occasionally ask yourself some questions: “Am I contributing enough?” “Am I still funding these accounts with the right mix of investments for my goals and risk tolerance?” But here’s one inquiry you might be overlooking: “Have I used the correct beneficiary designations?” And the answer you get is important. It wouldn’t be surprising if you haven’t thought much about the beneficiary designation – after all, it was just something you once signed, possibly a long time ago. Is it really that big a deal? It could be. For one thing, what if your family circumstances have changed since you named a beneficiary? If you’ve remarried, you may not want your former spouse to receive your IRA and 401(k) assets or the proceeds of your life insurance policy, for which you also named a beneficiary. However, upon remarrying, many people do review their estate plans, including their wills, living trusts, durable powers of attorney and health care directives. If you’ve revised these documents, do you have to worry about the old beneficiary designations? You might be surprised to learn that these previous designations can supersede what’s in your updated will and other documents. The end result could be an “accidental” inheritance in which your retirement accounts and insurance proceeds could end up going to someone who is no longer in your life. Furthermore, your retirement plans and insurance policy may not just require a single beneficiary – you may also be asked to name a contingent beneficiary, to whom assets will pass if the primary beneficiary has already died. As you can imagine, the situation could become quite muddled if stepchildren are involved in a remarriage. To avoid these potential problems, make sure to review the beneficiary designations on all of your accounts at some point – and especially after a significant change in your family situation. If you see something that is outdated or incorrect, contact your retirement account administrator – or your insurance representative, in the case of life insurance – to request a change-of-beneficiary form. And if you really want to be on the safe side, you may want to enlist a legal professional to help you with this review to make sure the beneficiary designations reflect your current family situation and are consistent with what’s in your estate plans. In fact, if you’re already working with an experienced estate planning attorney – and you should – you might also pick up some other suggestions for dealing with beneficiaries. Just to name one, it’s generally not a good idea to name minor children as beneficiaries. Because children can’t control the assets until they become adults, a court would likely have to name a guardian – one that you might not have wanted. Instead, you could either name your own custodian to manage the assets designated to the minor or establish a trust for the benefit of the minor, which can distribute the money in several disbursements over a period of years – which is often a good move, since young adults aren’t always the best at managing large lump sums. If you’re like many people, you have a strong desire to leave something behind. But you’ll want to do it in the right way. So, pay close attention to your beneficiary designations – when you first create them and throughout your life. Pictured are Albert Chen, Mark Davis, Noemi Alvarado, Barry Gantt, Jim Kuo, Melba Yee, Brenda Ferrero, Cheryl, Coleman Jones, Phil Witte, Priscilla Wanerus, Haybert Houston, Stella Houston, Quincy Dong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Carol Lyons, Adrienne Hamlin, Sherry Jacobs, Alan Goldhammer, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Olsen, Larry Olsen, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Alicia Rivera, and Nadine Guffanti. When members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays assembled at the Exedra on July 28, they were saddened to see the ad hoc memorial that community members had placed at the Exedra for the St. John family who had lost three of its four members in a tragic, deadly automobile accident in Minnesota on Sunday. The walk was led by Melba Yee, Priscilla Wanerus, and Albert Chen. Melba said the walkers in the past have explored many of the hidden stairways within Piedmont. Like Piedmont and Berkeley, Oakland has a series of hidden stairways that were developed with the residential development boom that occurred after the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco when people flocked to the East Bay. Developers built stairways so residents could get from the upper part of Piedmont to the lower parts of town and to have access the Key System trains. The stairways were part of the selling point for attracting buyers to the neighborhoods. Priscilla identified the Van Sicklen stairway in Oakland’s Crocker Highlands neighborhood near the Piedmont border as an opportunity to observe how some boundary lines were drawn and how the changes were reflected by the street, signage and homes in the area. Piedmont is unique in being perhaps the only city that is completely surrounded by another city. It has been referred to at times as Oakland’s “donut hole.” The borders of the town make no logical sense, as they do not appear to follow streets or physical landmarks. Boundary lines between the two cities sometimes cut through the middle of peoples’ homes, yards or businesses. In total there are 136 parcels that are partly in both Piedmont and Oakland. Some walkers were aware that in 1907 the town’s founding fathers had been in race to incorporate Piedmont as a separate city before Oakland could annex the area. In this rush, they used the only map they had for defining the boundaries – a sewer map that showed sewer lines snaking underneath the houses of Piedmont. The sewer map was not a good choice for setting jurisdictional boundaries, but once the boundaries were set, they could not be changed. The walkers set off on Highland Avenue to Sheridan, then to Wildwood and through the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. From Hampton, the group turned onto Indian Road. At the 200 block of Indian Road, the walkers noticed one of Piedmont’s Welcome to Piedmont signs facing in the opposite direction, The walkers knew that the sign meant that the walkers were now leaving Piedmont and entering Oakland. The walkers believed they might be on Sunnyhills Road, but that sign did not appear until the end of the block at the intersection with Downey Place. Walkers who lived in the Crocker Highlands neighborhood explained that Indian Road changed to Sunnyhills Road and that street names can change at places other than at an intersection. Continuing on Sunnyhills, they found Van Sicklen Place, a cul-de-sac where the first set of stairways descends to another cul-de-sac, Bowles Place. From there a steeper, longer stairway goes to Trestle Glen Road. The walkers continued down Sunnyhills Road, past Crocker Highlands Elementary School on Midcrest Road, to Longridge, Clarendon Crescent, and then to the Ashmount Farmer’s Market that operates out of a garage. The walkers had visited the market a few years ago and some members have since become regular customers. During the pandemic the market provided an alternative place to shop for those not comfortable with visiting large stores. The walkers also enjoyed seeing other homes near the market. Across from the market is a residence designed by the noted architect Bernard Maybeck. Next to the Maybeck house is a beautiful succulent garden that drew the attention of the walkers. All this exploration had made for an informative and enjoyable walk, but a little longer than usual for the group. They retraced their steps and made their way back to the Exedra. It had been about two hours and four miles of good exercise and time with Walking on Wednesdays friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the Group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Piedmont native Victoria Saykally found her passion for dentistry while completing her bachelor’s degree at the University of Washington. She discovered that dentistry allowed her to combine her love of art and interest in the sciences while also provide her with a platform to give back to her community. She studied Molecular, Cell, and Developmental Biology, as well as Global Health while working as a dental assistant. After completing her degree, Dr. Saykally worked as a research associate at a virology lab at UCSF, participating in the publication of multiple papers researching HIV and Cytomegalovirus. She went on to complete her doctorate degree at University of the Pacific in San Francisco. During this time, she led and participated in numerous dental outreach trips, both locally and abroad. She completed additional graduate training by completing a hospital-based residency at VA Victoria Saykally, DDS Palo Alto and Stanford. During the residency she focused on providing patient-centered comprehensive care to veterans, dental clearance for medically complex patients, and facial and dental emergency care to pediatric and adult patients. She is now with Ross Family Dentistry on Redwood Drive in Ross, in Marin County. Outside of dentistry, Dr. Saykally is an avid skier and hunter/jumper equestrian. articles.text: George H. Caig, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away at home on March 30, 2021 after living a long and very fulfilling life. He was 92. George, who many knew by his nickname Jud, was an incredible man – a caring and loving father, husband, grandfather, and great grandfather, and a good friend to many people. George was very appreciative of the beauty of nature and greatly enjoyed learning about plants, f lowers, and trees - locally and throughout his travels with his family, friends, and with his beloved wife, Julie. He was also a “green thumb” and enjoyed teaching his children about the greatness of the outdoors. He found fulfillment tending to his garden at their home in Piedmont. Born at Fabiola Hospital in Oakland, on July 8, 1928, George was raised in Piedmont and learned the value of creating stability and long-term planning due to his formative years during the Great Depression (1929-36). He went to Wildwood Elementary School and discovered his passion for exploring the outdoors by becoming an active member in the Boy Scouts, and eventually attaining the rank of Eagle Scout. He loved athletics, especially playing basketball and baseball. At Piedmont High School, Jud was an excellent basketball player and was known as a great long-range shooter. Jokingly, he referred to his best shots as, “punishing the nets” which he loved to do while playing a game of basketball in town - his favorite form of recreation into his late seventies. After graduating from Piedmont High School in 1946, George attended the University of California at Berkeley, where he advanced his business gent work in the Bond department, reviewing, detailing, and underwriting numerous mid-tolarge scale construction projects throughout the Bay Area and Northern California. Due to his George’s ability to plan, coupled with their desire to explore the world, Jud and Julie and their group of lifelong friends began to travel the globe. Their trips became a semi-annual event after planning sessions in Los Osos, CA. Their group toured Italy three times, Spain, Ireland, England, Scotland (where George’s ancestors built McCaig Tower long ago), France, Portugal, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, and many beautiful places throughout the United States. Jud and Julie’s favorite getaway closer to home was Mendocino. Jud never learned to play golf until after he retired, when he discovered his enjoyable, yet frustrating new hobby. Since he loved to walk and hike, and play sports, he quickly got hooked on a game that helped keep him active throughout his golden years. Volunteerism became a second calling during Jud’s retirement, and he cherished giving back some of his time and energy to those in need. He was honored to step up as a hardworking volunteer at Providence Hospital in Oakland for several years, and he assisted at the Piedmont Police Department to serve his hometown. George was a first-class person throughout his life. He was patient, humble, and a loving family man who always put his family first. He also treated his closest friends with the utmost love and respect and was there to assist whenever called upon. Jud will always be remembered for being an outstanding man, and for making the lives of his family and friends better than they could have imagined. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Rob Rich died on July 31 at his home in Danville. He was 71. Rob Rich, a former longtime Piedmont resident died in his sleep at his home in Danville in the early morning hours of July 31, 2021. He was 71. Born Robert Richard Rich on September 26, 1949 in Putnam, Connecticut, Rob was the only child of Joseph Reich and Lillian Whitehouse Rich. The family name was legally changed in the late 90s to Rich, to match the Polish pronunciation of the name. He grew up on a dairy farm, an experience that instilled in him a lifelong love for nature and animals. He became an Eagle Scout when he was 14 years old, when he matriculated at Pomfret School in Pomfret, Connecticut. Upon graduation, he attended Wesleyan University in Middletown, Conn., where he graduated in 1972. After working in the insurance industry and for an engineering company, Rob enrolled at Wharton Business School in Philadelphia. While there, he met Priscilla Chappell Dreby (Polly). They were married on June 17, 1978, and later that day got on a plane with their cat, Serena, and flew to San Francisco. They would live in the Bay Area their entire married life. Rob’s first job in California was at Del Monte, but after the company acquired R.J Reynolds, he was asked to move to North Carolina to work in the tobacco division. Rob had no desire to leave California or work for a company peddling cigarettes, and so took a job at McKesson. In 1992, he purchased a small wholesale business, Dan Gould & Sons, that sold soft goods to retail stores throughout the West Coast, primarily Longs Drugs. He very much enjoyed the work and took pride in being a small business owner, employing a diverse workforce headquartered in West Oakland. Rob and Polly became parents in 1983 with the birth of their son, Alexander, and later added to their family with the birth of their daughter, Kimberly. Until recently, their family always included at least one cat as well. They moved to Piedmont in 1985, and remained there until 2007, when they sold their home and moved to Danville. Rob passed on his love of sports and nature to his children by coaching their youth sports teams, serving as an adult leader for the Piedmont Boy Scout Council, taking them to the Sierra Nevada for cross country skiing, and taking trips to the East Coast that invariably included hiking, swimming, and boating in the Adirondacks. An avid Red Sox fan, Rob was in New England in October 2018 when the Curse of the Bambino was broken and the Sox won the World Series. He later became a cycling aficionado, enjoying the Tour de France, as well as cycling as many as 50 miles a day on his touring bike. He and Polly enjoyed and supported many local arts organizations, including San Francisco Ballet, California Shakespeare, Theatre Works, and Montalvo Arts. Travel to Muir Woods, Pt Reyes National Seashore, Yellowstone, Yosemite and international travel to Wimbledon, Mont Saint Michel, Montreal, and Vancouver BC were all life-enhancing adventures for both of them, often in the company of family and friends. After retiring from his soft goods business, Rob joined forces with Polly, becoming the CFO for her climate solutions-focused non-profit, Transition Express Inc. He gave her confidence, as a key board member, in finding meaningful ways to make a difference regarding the challenges posed by climate change. Rob is survived by his wife of 43 years, Polly; his son and daughter-in-law Alexander and Michelle Rich of Ukiah, CA; his daughter and son-in-law Kim and Jake Wallin of Chico, CA.; and his grandson, Damien Rich. He is preceded in death by his parents. Instead of recommended donations, we suggest supporting an arts organization of your choice that inspires you, and taking regular scenic hikes with a good friend.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Gifted educator, creative cook, passed on her love of life to her family Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully in Oakland, California on August 1, 2021. She was 94. Born in 1926 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Edward and Julia Lipman. When Margaret was five years old she contracted tuberculosis and was confined by doctors to bed rest for three years. She emerged from this confinement with an extraordinary joie de vivre. She attended Berkeley High School and graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, before getting a M.A. in Dramatic Arts from Columbia University in New York City. She also studied at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. Margaret met her future husband and true love of her life, John Pillsbury, when she was in nursery school with his younger sister, Susan. The comment was made that when Margaret and John married in 1950, half of Berkeley became related. Margaret and John enjoyed a wonderful and much-admired marriage for 52 years. Margaret was a great believer in the power of education and was a life-long learner, as well as a dedicated teacher. She taught in Oakland public schools for over 20 years and inspired and encouraged many future teachers, including her daughter Karen Austin, daughter-in-law Megan Pillsbury, and granddaughter Amelia Dufrechou. After “retirement” Margaret taught English as a Second Language (ESL) at the elementary school level and was a docent at the Oakland Museum and the Phoebe Hearst Anthropology Museum. And after a second “retirement” Margaret became a much-loved Adult ESL teacher at Piedmont Adult School and the Downtown Oakland Senior Center, and taught well into her 90’s. She was well known and widely respected for her creative approach to teaching language using food as the common focus of learning. Her ESL students in Piedmont celebrated the end of the semester with a student-prepared feast as part of the final exam. Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully at age 94 on August 1, 2021. She is pictured with her husband John Pillsbury. Margaret will be remembered for her great zest for life, a love of travel and other cultures, and a special fondness for the arts. Margaret was an enthusiastic supporter of Berkeley Rep, Cal Performances, the San Francisco Symphony, the DeYoung Museum, the Asian Art Museum, the Oakland Symphony, and the Oakland Museum. She and John travelled to many places in the world, including Peru, where they assisted their youngest daughter Joanne on an archeological dig she was directing. Margaret shared her love of travel with her children, who have many family stories including one about a beer-drinking burro in Mexico. She was a supporter of progressive causes and once instructed Joe Biden about the meaning of César Chávez’s UFW motto of “Sí, Se Puede” or “Yes We Can” – coined 30 years before the Obama presidential campaign. As “Nana”, Margaret was grandmother to seven grandchildren and one great-grandson. She loved holidays and celebrated with great delight Three Kings Day, Chinese New Year, Cinco de Mayo, Bastille Day and Day of the Dead, in addition to Thanksgiving, Christmas, Easter, and Fourth of July. Margaret was an adventurous cook and embraced Julia Child early on, but ultimately her cook’s heart belonged to Jacques Pepin. Her grandchildren will remember her wonderful roast chicken, her spicy lemonade, her early adoption of quinoa, her favorite drinking toasts in both French and Spanish, and the Che Guevara socks she wore to Alycia’s Heartbeat exercise class which she attended for 36 years. Margaret is survived by her children: Karen Austin of Alameda, Tom Pillsbury and wife Megan of Piedmont, Jim Pillsbury and wife Noelle of Piedmont, and Joanne Pillsbury Harwood and husband Edward of Manhattan and Maine. She is also survived by grandchildren Nicholas McMahon (Kelly), Timothy Austin McMahon, Amelia Dufrechou (Max), Claire Pillsbury, Jack Pillsbury, Alec Pillsbury, Colin Pillsbury; and great-grandson Elliot Dufrechou. Margaret is predeceased by her husband John, her sisters Jean and Kathryn, and her son Mark who died in infancy. The family thanks all her caregivers and the staff at St. Paul’s Towers for their wonderful care and support. We will celebrate Margaret at a future date. In the meantime, please raise a glass and toast “!Salud, amor, pesetas, y el tiempo para disfrutarlos!” Margaret Pilllsbury in Florence, Italy after the war in 1948. As a newlywed, Margaret Pillsbury discovered the joys of hiking.
